pages.text: Efua had a plan. Her grandmother made the best groundnut cakes in the neighbourhood, and Efua had asked to learn the recipe. If she could sell twenty packs after school each day, she might earn enough to pay for her own school supplies.
sentences: Efua had a plan.
Her grandmother made the best groundnut cakes in the neighbourhood, and Efua had asked to learn the recipe.
If she could sell twenty packs after school each day, she might earn enough to pay for her own school supplies.
pages.alt: A thirteen-year-old girl in a school uniform kneels beside her grandmother, who shows her how to shape groundnut cakes.

pages.text: She did the arithmetic carefully in her exercise book. The ingredients for twenty packs cost twelve cedis. If she sold each pack for one cedi, she would make eight cedis profit. ‘Eight cedis a day,’ she whispered. ‘That is forty cedis a week.’
sentences: She did the arithmetic carefully in her exercise book.
The ingredients for twenty packs cost twelve cedis.
If she sold each pack for one cedi, she would make eight cedis profit.
‘Eight cedis a day,’ she whispered.
‘That is forty cedis a week.’
pages.alt: Efua writes calculations in an exercise book at a table.

pages.text: On Monday she sold fourteen packs. On Tuesday she sold sixteen. People said the cakes were crunchy, fresh and not too sweet. But on Wednesday, Kwabena pulled her aside near the school gate.
sentences: On Monday she sold fourteen packs.
On Tuesday she sold sixteen.
People said the cakes were crunchy, fresh and not too sweet.
But on Wednesday, Kwabena pulled her aside near the school gate.
pages.alt: Efua sells small packs of groundnut cakes to students at the school gate.

pages.text: ‘You are wasting money,’ said Kwabena. ‘Use cheaper oil, and put fewer groundnuts in each pack. Nobody will notice. And tell people they are fresh today, even if you made them yesterday. You will make twice the profit.’
sentences: ‘You are wasting money,’ said Kwabena.
‘Use cheaper oil, and put fewer groundnuts in each pack.
Nobody will notice.
And tell people they are fresh today, even if you made them yesterday.
You will make twice the profit.’
pages.alt: Kwabena speaks quietly to Efua, leaning in, while she looks uncertain.

pages.text: Efua did the sums again that night. Kwabena was right about one thing: she could make more. But she kept thinking about her customers. They trusted her, and trust, she realised, was worth more than eight cedis a day.
sentences: Efua did the sums again that night.
Kwabena was right about one thing: she could make more.
But she kept thinking about her customers.
They trusted her, and trust, she realised, was worth more than eight cedis a day.
pages.alt: Efua sits by lamplight with her exercise book, thinking.

pages.text: The next morning she visited Auntie Dede, who sold vegetables at the market. ‘Customers are like a garden,’ said Auntie Dede. ‘Treat them well and they return all year. Cheat them once and they will remember it forever.’
sentences: The next morning she visited Auntie Dede, who sold vegetables at the market.
‘Customers are like a garden,’ said Auntie Dede.
‘Treat them well and they return all year.
Cheat them once and they will remember it forever.’
pages.alt: A market trader speaks kindly to Efua among baskets of vegetables.

pages.text: Efua kept her recipe honest. She even added a few extra groundnuts to every pack and began to write the day each batch was made on a small label. Some days she made less profit. But the line at the school gate grew longer.
sentences: Efua kept her recipe honest.
She even added a few extra groundnuts to every pack and began to write the day each batch was made on a small label.
Some days she made less profit.
But the line at the school gate grew longer.
pages.alt: Efua adds extra groundnuts to a pack and writes the date on a small label.

pages.text: By the end of the month, Efua was selling twenty-five packs a day. Even Kwabena stood in the queue one afternoon. ‘You were right about one thing,’ he admitted. ‘Honesty is slower, but it lasts longer.’ Efua smiled and handed him his pack.
sentences: By the end of the month, Efua was selling twenty-five packs a day.
Even Kwabena stood in the queue one afternoon.
‘You were right about one thing,’ he admitted.
‘Honesty is slower, but it lasts longer.’ Efua smiled and handed him his pack.
pages.alt: A long line of students at the school gate; Kwabena at the end of the queue and Efua handing him a pack.

activities.question: How much profit did Efua expect to make each day from twenty packs?
activities.explanation: She would earn twenty cedis but spend twelve on ingredients, so the profit is eight cedis.

activities.question: What did Efua mean when she realised that trust was worth more than eight cedis a day?
options: Keeping customers’ trust could earn more over time than cheating them once
Eight cedis is a very small amount
activities.explanation: She understood that customers who trust her will return for longer.

items: Efua works out her costs and profit.
